claims.text: Existing tungsten/tantalum-containing refractory high-entropy alloys have excellent high-temperature mechanical properties.
Existing tungsten/tantalum-containing refractory high-entropy alloys have strong irradiation resistance.
Tungsten and tantalum create high-activation issues in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Vanadium, chromium, and titanium are lower-activation alternatives to tungsten and tantalum.
Fusion plasma-facing materials must operate at temperatures of at least 1000 K.
Fusion plasma-facing components experience intense neutron irradiation and plasma exposure.
Low activation is a stringent requirement for fusion plasma-facing materials.
Compositional tuning of the proposed refractory high-entropy alloy will stabilize its microstructural phases.
The proposed compositional tuning will preserve beneficial nanostructuring and phase integrity.
Replacing tungsten and tantalum with lower-activation elements will reduce production of long-lived radioisotopes under neutron irradiation.
The multi-principal-element nature of high-entropy alloys suppresses irradiation-induced defects.
Enhanced defect suppression and phase stability allow high-entropy alloys to retain high-temperature mechanical performance and irradiation resistance.
The modified refractory high-entropy alloy will have significantly lower long-term radioactive activation than a tungsten-based control.
The modified refractory high-entropy alloy will retain mechanical strength and irradiation resistance comparable to the tungsten-based control.
The modified refractory high-entropy alloy will be suitable for high-temperature plasma-facing applications.
Traditional tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys offer excellent thermal performance.
Traditional tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys generate undesirable long-lived radioactive activation products.
The proposed benefit depends on substitution not compromising melting point, phase stability, or high-temperature mechanical properties.
The quantitative trade-offs between activation reduction and changes in mechanical or thermal properties are uncertain until tested under reactor-like conditions.
Failure to reduce long-lived activation, or degradation of mechanics or irradiation resistance below acceptable control levels, would falsify the hypothesis.
